E-Selective N-Heterocyclic Carbene-Catalyzed 
Reaction of Aldehydes and Butadienoates: Effect of 
Water and Chloroform as the Proton Shuttle  
Dengke Ma, a Yulong Song, a Chunling Fu, a Fang Zhang, b Yinlong Guo, b Xin Huang* ,a and 
Shengming Ma* ,a 
As we know, there are many reports on the reactions of the Breslow intermediate with 
electron(deficient alkenes or alkynes. However, the reactions with allenes are much less 
studied.
 In this study we observed that  N(heterocyclic carbene(catalyzed reaction of aldehydes 
and butadienoates afforded  (E)(4(oxo(2(butenoates highly stereoselectively. It was observed 
that addition of water is critical for the observed high stereoselectivity. Mechanistic studies 
showed that the solvent chloroform acted as the proton shuttle involved in the formation of the 
Breslow intermediate, protonation, and deprotonation for this carbene(catalyzed reaction. 
Some key intermediates such as the Breslow intermediate and its mono hydrate have been 
detected and characterized by MS studies, supporting the proposed mechanism. 
 
 
Introduction 
The Breslow intermediate formed from the reaction of simple 
aldehydes and carbenes, firstly disclosed in 1958,
1 was 
ubiquitously involved in many N(heterocyclic carbene(
catalyzed reactions. Ever since its discovery, studies on the 
mechanism have always been on a par with development of 
corresponding new transformations.
2 A proton transfer process, 
mediated by base, 3 H 2O,3 conjugate acid, 4 or intramolecular 
1,2(hydrogen shift, 5 and even intermolecular proton transfer 
involving two NHC/aldehyde adducts, 4a,6 after the primary 1,2(
addition of N(heterocyclic carbene with aldehyde in the 
formation of the Breslow intermediate have been reported. 
Apart from that, the spiroepoxide intermediate
7 and radical 
mechanism8 were also proposed. On the other hand, in 2012, 
Berkessel et al. pioneeringly characterized the 2,2(diamino 
enols by NMR spectroscopy and it was proved that the α(proton 
of aldehyde is proven to be the source of hydroxylic proton in 
the Breslow intermediate (Scheme 1A, eq. 1).
9,10 Recently, we 
reported a N(heterocyclic carbene(catalyzed cyclization 
reaction of aldehydes and 1,2(allenones affording cyclopent(2(
enone(4(ols 
S1 with high diastereoselectivity referring to the 
two chiral centers. 11 The intermediate Int-I with Z(
configuration formed after the addition of the Breslow 
intermediate with 1,2(allenone was believed to be crucial for 
the subsequent cyclization (Scheme 1B, eq. 2). What’s more, 
when 
α(deuteriobenzaldehyde was submitted to the reaction, 
deuterated product was afforded smoothly, confirming the 
proton transfer process as in reported literatures. 9 Interestingly, 
when butadienoates were used as the coupling partners with the 
Breslow intermediate in the presence of water, (
E)(4(oxo(2(
butenoates ( E)(3 were formed highly stereoselectively: the 
formation of stereoisomer ( Z)(4(oxo(2(butenoate ( Z)(3 and 
double bonds isomer 4 are negligible. These results illustrated 
the entirely different intermediate Int-II with the E(
configuration after the addition of the Breslow intermediate 
with butadienoates (Scheme 1B, eq. 3). In addition, besides the 
Breslow intermediate formed in the similar manner as that 
Berkessel et al. reported (Scheme 1C, path a),
9 we also 
observed a rather unexpected phenomenon: the primary adduct 
of 
N(heterocyclic carbene with aldehyde was most probably 
protonated with the solvent(chloroform, led to the 
transformation with chloroform as the proton shuttle (Scheme 
1C, eq. 4) and the formation of the monohydrated Breslow 
intermediate is responsible for the observed stereoselectivity as 
supported by MS studies (Scheme 1C, eq. 5). We wish to report 
here these observations.

Results and discussion 
Initially, we attempted the reaction of benzaldehyde 1a with 
butadienoate 2a in the presence of 20 mol% 1(ethyl(3(
methylimidazolium tetrafluoroborate (EMIMBF 4) and 20 mol% 
Cs2CO3 in toluene at (10 oC. Disappointingly, no product was 
obtained with 84% recovery of 2a (Table 1, entry 1). Gladly, 
the formation of 3aa was observed in dioxane or THF at 20 oC 
with full consumption of 2a, however, the stereoselectivity is 
poor (Table 1, entries 2 and 3). When DCM was used as the 
solvent, (E)(3aa was formed as the sole product in 42% yield 
with 22% recovery of 2a (Table 1, entry 4). At last, we were 
very pleased to find that running the reaction in commercial 
CHCl3 under 30 mol% of Cs 2CO3 gave the best results: the 
yield of ( E)(3aa was 61% with exclusive E selectivity while 
4aa was formed in only 1% yield with full conversion of 2a 
(Table 1, entry 5). 
When 1.8 equiv of 1a were used, the stereoselectivity of 3aa 
was somewhat improved. Thus, the reaction was optimized 
with 1.8 equiv of 
1a. Quite unexpectedly, control experiments 
showed that reactions carried out in commercial CHCl 3 and 
anhydrous CHCl 3 (distilled from CaH 2 under N 2 before use) 
gave rather different results: the stereoselectivity and yield of 
3aa in anhydrous CHCl 3 dropped to 92/8 and 61%, and 4aa 
was formed in 7% yield, which indicated the potential role of 
water in the commercial CHCl

Based on these mechanistic studies, we proposed a possible 
reaction mechanism for the formation of ( E)(3aa-D in CDCl 3. 
N(Heterocyclic carbene generated in situ  would react with 
benzaldehyde 1a in the presence of water to form 
monohydrated Breslow intermediate  1-A. Then intermeidate 1-
A would react with 2a to form a delocalized anionic 
intermediate 1-B11,13 due to the steric effect. Intermediate 1-B 
would be protonated with CDCl 3 to form intermediate 1-C or 1-
D. Subsequently, in the presence of Cs 2CO3 or trichloromethide 
carbanion, intermediate 1-C would be deprotonated at the 
hydroxyl group to give intermediate 1-F. Subsequent 
elimination of N(heterocyclic carbene would generate ( E)(3aa-
D and regenerate the carbene (Scheme 3, path a). The active 
methylene unit in intermediate 1-D would be deprotonated to 
yield intermediate 1-E by N(heterocyclic carbene 14 or Cs 2CO3. 
Then intermediate 1-E was protonated by CDCl 3 to from 
intermediate 1-C’. In the presence of Cs 2CO3 or 
trichloromethide carbanion, intermediate 1-C’ would also be 
transferred to intermediate 1-F (Scheme 3, path b). 
(E)(4(Oxo(2(butenoates have been proven to be important 
motifs of some bioactive compounds, natural products, and 
macrocyclic antibiotics, such as pyrenophorin and vermiculin.
15

transformations, such as Diels(Alder reaction,
16 cyclization, 17 
cyclopropanation,18 addition reactions as Michael acceptors, 19 
etc., affording a series of carbocycles, heterocycles and other 
polyfunctional structures. Thus, these compounds are attracting 
continuous interest. So far, many methods have been developed 
for the preparation of (
E)(4(oxo(2(butenoates.20 However, these 
methods usually suffer from unsatisfactory stereoselectivity, 
low atom economy, non(readily(available starting materials, 
using stoichiometric or toxic reagents in some cases. Therefore,

Conclusions 
In conclusion, mechanistic studies show that N(heterocyclic 
carbene may react with the aldehydes in the presence of water 
to afford the monohydrated Breslow intermediate and the 
solvent CHCl
3 acts as the proton shuttle. Subsequent 
thermodynamically controlled Michael addition with 
butadienates, repeated protonation and deprotonation involving 
CHCl3 and water, and elimination yielded the final products. 
Based on this, we have also developed an efficient reaction for 
the preparation of (
E)(4(oxo(2(butenoates from readily 
available aromatic aldehydes and butadienoates with a high 
stereoselectivity and atom economy. Further investigation 
including reactions of other electron(deficient allenes catalyzed 
by NHC is being carried out in our laboratory.
